result.question: Temple architecture in south India attained its climax under the Cholas. Discuss the main features of the Dravida style with suitable examples. (Answer in 250 words)

directives.meaning: Look at the issue from more than one side, with reasons, and reach a balanced view.

sentences.text: The Dravida style of temple architecture, which took shape under the Pallavas, reached its climax under the imperial Cholas.
It is so called because it was largely confined to south India.
Its defining feature is the vimana, a pyramidal tower of several storeys rising above the garbhagriha that houses the main deity.
A mandapa with elaborately carved pillars and a flat roof, placed in front of the sanctum, served as an audience hall and a venue for ritual dances by devadasis.
The complex, often with a circumambulatory passage around the sanctum, was enclosed by high walls pierced by gateways called gopurams, which became ever more elaborate in later centuries.
An early example is the eighth-century Kailasanatha temple at Kanchipuram, built by the Pallava ruler Rajasimha.
The Brihadeshwara temple at Thanjavur, built by Rajaraja I and also called the Rajarajeshwara temple, is among the finest expressions of the style, with a towering vimana over its sanctum.
Rajendra I's temple at his new capital, Gangaikondacholapuram, and Rajaraja II's Airavateshvara temple at Darasuram continued this tradition.
Temples were also economic hubs, receiving revenue-free land grants and merchant donations, lending money and funding tanks and irrigation channels.
In Karnataka, the Hoysaleswara temple at Halebidu, with its richly carved panels, exemplifies a hybrid Deccan style often classed as Vesara.

As living shrines and centres of community life, Chola temples integrated architecture, sculpture, painting and dance, and their heritage deserves sustained conservation and wider public appreciation.
